utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Good morning, Professor Wagenaar. I would like to ask you to make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may be seated. Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Wagenaar. Do you hear me well, Professor? To begin with, Professor, I should like to ask you, for the record, to give us your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Willem Albert Wagenaar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be kind enough to convey to the Court some information about your professional career, the posts you have held in the past and that you are holding at present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am an experimental psychologist, and experimental psychology deals with the general psychological faculties that humans have, like perception, visual perception, auditory perception, memory, and general capabilities like that. I was first trained at Utrecht University and defended my dissertation at Leiden University. From there on, I worked for 20 years in the Institute for Perception, TNO, which is a separate research institute in the Netherlands that deals with mostly questions of perception, and face perception is one of the topics that I addressed there. From 1974 till 1985, I held the post of head of the psychology department in that institute. In 1983, I was appointed as a partial professor at the University of Leiden, and in 1985 I moved completely to the University of Leiden, where I held the post of experimental psychology. From 1987 till 1989, I was dean of the faculty of social sciences, and, now, from 1997 till today, I am the vice-chancellor -- or, as we say, the rector magnificus, of Leiden University.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Professor, could you now tell us briefly something about your scientific work, the papers you have published in your field and some of the studies you have done in the area of human perception.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. By now I have published more than 150 publications. Many of them deal with problems of perception and problems of memory, in which the question usually is the problem of remembering what you saw. Many of these publications are in the context, or immediately inspired, even, by problems that occur in the judicial process, like processes of, say, what witnesses can see, what witnesses can or do remember, what the reliability of eyewitness testimony is. I have published several books on this problem, again, usually inspired by very concrete trials in which such questions were asked to me. I have acted as an expert witness on such questions in, I estimate, more than 200 trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Among other things, you have also testified in this International Tribunal, I believe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have testified in the Tadic case, which I think was one of the first trials that took place in this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now that we have learned, at least in broad lines, something about your professional activities and scientific work, can we go on to your expert opinion provided for the needs of this trial. To facilitate your presentation, I should like to provide Their Honours and the parties a copy of your expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I should like to ask the usher for his assistance to help me distribute these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D58/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Professor, upon the request of the Defence of the accused, Vlatko Kupreskic, you have provided your expert opinion on the identification of Vlatko Kupreskic by Witness Q. Could you please tell us what kind of information and data that you obtained from the Defence, you used when providing your expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I received, from the Defence, an introducing letter explaining what the problem was they wanted me to address, and as I have here a partial copy of the trial record that represents -- which is the most important for me -- some statements by the Witness Q and some other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. To have a more complete idea as to the kind of letter that you used, I should again ask the usher to help me provide Their Honours and the Office of the Prosecutor with a copy of that letter. Talking about this letter, Professor, you said that it contained a certain number of data which you used when drawing up your expert opinion. I would suggest that I read out that part from the letter containing that information, the initial situation that we described in that letter in which the recognition took place. As Their Honours have a copy of that letter, and the Prosecutor, let me just read the part that is relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D59/3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could a copy be placed on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: The letter describes how the Defence presented the situation under which recognition was carried out, and so I'm reading from the letter. The event and the conditions under which recognition took place, according to the statements of the witness whose testimony we are interested in, were the following: "During the military activities in a Bosnian village on the 16th of April, 1993, around 9 a.m., a group consisting of several civilians -- women, children, and elderly people -- fled from their homes in order to save their lives. Shooting from light and heavy weapons was in course for several hours. Murders and burning of houses were ongoing, and the group decided to save themselves by escape. The group was moving along a sheltered part of the terrain. Then they climbed a small hill, and, at that point, they came out on terrain where they were spotted by enemy soldiers. The group at that point was faced away from the soldiers. They had their backs turned on the soldiers, and in one moment they heard loud swearing and threats coming from the soldiers. The group turned around for a moment. They looked at the soldiers, who were standing approximately 60 metres away from them, and in that moment, the soldiers started to shoot at the group. On that occasion, one person was killed and two persons wounded." That is the part of the letter which we sent to you, and in which we, as the Defence, described the situation as we assumed it was. In continuation of this letter or, rather, our request for your expert opinion, we have asked eight specific questions. That is, we asked you to give us your expert opinion regarding eight factors which could have affected the reliability of the identification. In your written opinion, you responded to each of these points, so I should like to ask you to present those answers yourself, directly, in this courtroom. Would you please begin your presentation with the first part of your finding, where you noted that there were two different modes of identification, person identification, and could you describe briefly both modes and then tell us which were the points that we set and what your expert opinion about them is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally, there are two situations in which a problem of person identification may occur. One is the situation in which a witness recognises a person known to him or her already before the time of the crime. So that's the problem of identifying, recognising, a well-known person. That process can be very fast. In a flash, you may recognise someone whom you have known all your life, for instance. Later on, the only thing you have to remember is the fact that you recognised that person. You don't have to remember, say, the whole image of that event. It is sufficient, for instance, to recall, to remember, the name of the person you have recognised. That's situation 1. Situation 2 is when, during a crime, you are faced with a person you have never seen before, so you can't try to remember the name of that person because you don't know that person. Then, usually later on, for instance, in an identity test, you are again confronted with that person or a number of persons in a line-up, and the question is whether you recognise that person. In order to do that, it is necessary that you have stored, from the time of the crime on, an image of the person you saw, because in your head you have to compare the image that you saw originally with the image of the person you see now. Now, these two processes are entirely different, and the factors that influence the one are not necessarily the same as the factors that influence the other. Now, in the case we are discussing today, we are dealing with situation 1. The task was to recognise a person that was supposedly known to the witness long before. So the factors that are relevant in this case are the factors that influence the immediate recognition process. The problem of recall, of remembering, is minute, is very small, because the only thing that had to be remembered, in fact, is the name of the person who was seen there at the scene of the crime. So factors that influence remembering or forgetting are probably not very relevant because the task to the witness was only to remember the name of the person he saw. So decisive factors are factors that influence perception, recognition on the spot, and not factors that deteriorate your memory, because the memory task is very slight. Now, in the list of eight questions that you gave me, some of the questions are in fact addressing the perception situation and are therefore highly relevant, and some address the problem of remembering and are therefore probably not so relevant. So that's the distinction that I made. Now, in my letter to you, I started to explain that in my opinion, the most relevant factor is, in this case, the observation distance, which was presented to me as being in the order of 60 metres. That is a highly-relevant factor, because if you are at such a distance that you can't see the face of a person, then everything else stops, then there is nothing to put into your memory. There's no memory problem also. The first question to be addressed is is it possible to recognise a person known to you, known very well to you, at a distance of 60 metres in such a way that we can safely say that no mistake is possible. Now, at this point there is a problem that can only be solved by the Court, and that is how reliable should such a recognition be. Some experimental data that I have provided to you is that under optimal conditions, to our best knowledge, the chances that you recognise a familiar person at a distance of about 60 metres are something like 50 per cent correct, 50 per cent wrong, or worse, that that would probably be the best performance. So I'm not saying that you cannot recognise a person at 60 metres, but I am saying that 50 per cent wrong is not highly reliable in a legal sense. It is quite possible that the person would make a mistake. In my opinion, it would be at least as likely that the person makes a mistake as that the person would be correct. Now, whether that level of reliability is good enough for the Court, I cannot decide. I can only give the information. Now, if I want to go into some detail, I would like to explain that we are confronted here with a biological fact. Our eyes are built to perceive, and inside the eye, say the area where, say, the light hits the receptor is called the retina, and the retina contains a very large number of small receptors called cones, and the cones are placed in some sort of mosaic pattern, and it is clear that a detail that is smaller than a cone cannot be clearly resolved, as we say it, by the retina. A detail needs to cover at least one cone, but it would be a lot better if it would cover a number of cones so that the shape of that detail will be perceived. Now, the density of cones, the number of cones on a square millimetre, is a biological fact and is almost invariably the same for all people. It's not the same for all living beings. Eagles have a much denser placement of cones and they can see a lot more details. But humans are not eagles. The density of cones in the human eye is the same for all persons, with very slight variations. Another fact is that the details in a human face that you need to see in order to make sure that this is the one person, not the other person, are in the order of half a centimetre. If you can't see differences of half a centimetre, then you confuse the one shape of an eye with another shape of an eye, the one shape of a nose with another shape of a nose. In order to recognise a person, you need to see details of about half a centimetre, and if the distance, the observation distance, is so large that half a centimetre on a face falls just within one cone, then you cannot resolve these details anymore, you cannot see them, and it becomes rather tricky to recognise a person. These results are confirmed in a number of studies, and I've done some of these studies myself, and it is quite obvious that the details that the eye can see at a distance of 60 metres are in the order of two centimetres, not smaller, and definitely not half a centimetre, and that's why, at a distance of 60 metres, it becomes rather likely that you will make mistakes. I'm still not saying that you can't recognise a person at 60 metres, I'm only saying the likelihood of mistakes become rather high. Now, what I'm telling you is related to optimal viewing conditions like perfect daylight, you have all the time that you want, there is no haze, no fog, no smoke. All these other factors can make it more difficult to recognise a person. If there's no perfect daylight, if there is smoke, if you see the person for a very short time, all that makes it more difficult. But even under optimal conditions, the likelihood of a mistake would be rather high.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. If I may interrupt you just for a moment. Could you please tell us, this percentage of error, how does it grow with distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my letter to you, I gave you a small table that is based on my own research, and if you take the last column of that table with the heading "3.000," and "3.000" refers to the elimination level and "3.000" represents a normal day, somewhat clouded but normal daylight, and then the numbers in that table give you the ratio of correct answers to incorrect answers. So, for instance, in the second row, if it says "108," then there are 108 correct answers to one wrong. So these numbers are odds, the odds of making a correct identification. Now what you see is that at 3, 5, 7, and 12 metres, the odds of making a correct identification are rather high; 27, 108, 55, 90. There is always some variation because these are experimental data, not theoretical data. And suddenly at 20, it drops to below 5. That sudden drop represents the moment where suddenly the details of half a centimetre fall within the area of one cone in the retina. If they fall over several cones, there is no problem and distance is not even so important. But at the critical point somewhere between 12 and 20 metres, the details become too small, and then the ability to recognise a person suddenly drops. I have never done distances longer than 40 metres because, from this table, it's quite clear that at 40 metres the likelihood of making errors is already so large that it would be useless to research longer distances.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: That is just what I wanted to ask you, "Why don't you go further, after 40 metres," so now you have given us the explanation for this procedure. I interrupted you, Professor. When you were talking about other factors influencing perception, you mentioned the distance, the lighting and other circumstances. So please continue, and I apologise for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this far I have discussed, in fact, your question number 3, and I took that first because I think that observation distance is the most crucial in this case. If you now go back to question number 1, the fact that the witness was in life danger, in our research, we call this the factor of the presence of emotions, and what I have explained to you in my letter is that emotions can have two effects, or generally it's assumed that emotion has the effect that your field of attention becomes smaller. You focus your attention upon one thing, the one thing that's most crucial to you. The fact then of emotion can be that you perceive that one thing better, and you may also remember that better. In that sense, emotion can improve the observation. But if you focus your attention on a particular thing at the same time, naturally you don't pay attention to some other things, and the likelihood that you will perceive those other things and remember them becomes smaller. So the effect of emotions mean generally that you will remember some things better and other things worse. The only question is where did you fixate, what was important for you at that time, and it's very hard to tell because a person under high emotions is not so rational. What will be selected as the thing to focus at might not always be what is the most relevant at the time of a trial. So it's very hard to say what emotions in this present case would have done. My science doesn't give me enough guidance to say whether emotions would have helped or would have had the opposite effect. The question number 2 relates to the fact that the witness looked just for one moment. Well, in principle, you can recognise a person in one eye fixation, and you can make one eye fixation in half a second, and I would say one moment probably is at least half a second. That should be enough for recognising a person that you know so very well. So that should not be a problem, in principle. Question number 3, I answered already. Question number 4 is the problem that the person who was recognised, whoever he was, was standing in a group, so there was more to see than just that one person. Now, what I reckoned in my letter, that if this were a closed group of people, standing together, then, at a distance of 60 metres, you don't need more than one fixation to see the whole group. If you look at one point, there's a certain area around that point that we can see without moving our eyes; we call that the stationary field. Other things, outside this stationary field, can only be seen if we move our eyes, and eye fixations take time. So the larger the group, the more fixations you need to make and the more time you need. But if four persons stand closely together, they can be seen in one eye fixation, and the fact that there is a whole group doesn't matter so much; they can be seen all at the same time. So that, in principle, should not be a problem. Question number 5 was the age of Witness Q. Now, age-related eyesight problems are usually problems of reading, problems of seeing at a very short distance; usually the eyesight for a long distance remains the same. I say "usually" because of course there are individual differences. But without further information about Witness Q, I can only say, if he is a normal person, at 55 he will have already some reading problems and probably needs eyeglasses for reading, but not for a distance. If the opposite is claimed, the obvious solution, to find an answer to this question, is to send him to an ophthalmologist and ask him to study his eyes. I can only tell you what usually would happen, so I would say that the age of Witness Q with respect to his eyesight is probably not relevant. Question Number 6, the fact that other persons who were also watching the scene couldn't recognise anyone, well, what I explained in my letter, I'm not surprised at that, because, in fact, I do not expect that people would correctly recognise another person at a distance of 60 metres, so the fact that the others didn't recognise anyone needs no further explanation. What we need to explain, how it was possible that one of them still, at a distance, recognised someone. So there is no real conflict. Of course they didn't recognise anyone. Seven -- and here we go into the memory problem -- the fact that Witness Q could not explain what kind of clothing the person he saw, and he said he recognised, was wearing. Well, in order to recognise him at that time, on the spot, he didn't need to pay attention to the clothing of that person; the face is, of course, the most important thing if you want to recognise anyone. And for remembering who he saw, he only needed to remember the name of the person. It's not necessary at all that he also remembered the image that he saw, so that later on he could tell you, "On that image of this person, I can now also tell you which clothes he was wearing." So, given that the clothes of this person were probably not relevant to him at all -- usually the weapon is the most important thing, and then the face, but the clothing is not relevant -- and the fact that in order to make his testimony he needed only to remember the name of that person, it's not surprising that after some time, when he finally made his testimony, he didn't remember the clothing. So that's not a problem. Question Number 8 is a rather complicated question, and if I may, I need some time to explain why that is complicated, because Question 8 is related to what I say, as a general term, called "suggestion." If we see something that is not very clear and we store the unclear information in our heads, then it's quite possible that what we call "post-event information," information that reaches us afterwards, will sharpen that image, will affect that image, and also may change that image, because the image of what we saw, in our heads, is not stable at all but is constantly reprocessed in the context of knowledge that we receive. Human memory is not like a video recorder, where the recording stays unchanged. Human memory is very active, is very much alive, and information that we have is not simply stored and recalled when we need it; no, it's constantly processed in the context of knowledge that we receive. That's very useful for people, very useless for a court, because we would rather like witnesses to be like video recorders, but unfortunately, they are not. Now, your question is the fact that later on, the witness received information about the person he recognised -- now living in his house, if I am correct -- may have affected the image that he remembered, and I can, of course, not describe what happened; I can only describe what may happen in a person. I must say the most important condition for post-event-information-induced changes to occur is that the first observation is not totally clear. If I have a totally clear initial observation, probably there's no new information that may change that, but if it's not clear, if it's vague, then there is an opportunity for what you may call a sharpening of the image as a consequence of receiving new information. Now, what I would say is that seeing a person at 60 metres creates not a sharp image of a particular face, because the critical details are not resolved in the retina. It creates a vague image that may be recognised correctly, but also maybe is confused with another person. Now, that vague image is a perfect basis for post-event information to have an effect, and I listed in my letter a number of pieces of information that could have such effect, like the fact they were standing in front of a certain house, or some facts that are known about the accused -- that he belongs to some group, or that he might have had a weapon; all sorts of information that may come later may influence that image. It is very hard to limit the sort of information that can have that effect, and I'm not perfectly aware of all the information that has been presented to Witness Q about the accused, so it's very hard for me to even guess what has happened. I only can say that the starting position of a vague image, seen at a distance of 60 metres, is a good starting point for suggestive post-event information to have effect. Now, an important aspect here is that if you have a very clear image, you can also say immediately whom you have recognised. Recognition is usually a process that happens very quickly. You see something. You say, "I know who that is." Recognition is not something that is spread out over a month, so that first, you didn't know it; after several months, you know it. That process, very gradually, you start to realise what or whom you saw, is totally different from immediate perception. It is a construction. When you start to realise, you use all sorts of information to make the vague image that you have in your head sharper, and at the end, you know -- "Ah, but now I know what that vague image in fact means." But that's not perception; that is reconstruction, and reconstruction is very much influenced by information that you receive during that period. So the two important elements here, although I cannot answer your question whether suggestion has occurred, but the two important elements are the initial position is good for suggestion, because it's a vague image, and as far as I could tell from the information that I received, recognition was not immediate. It was a process that took a while, and only after a certain amount of time, Witness Q testified that he knew who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I have a question with regard to that. I'm interested in knowing -- let us assume, under suggestion, some kind of suggestion, the suggestion we talked about a moment ago, if he performs identification, I'm interested whether that individual intimately believes that he is speaking the truth and has had a clear identification, the subjective views of that individual that they have recognised the person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. That's an important aspect of all eyewitness testimony, the certainty, the conviction that the eyewitness has, the sincere and strong belief that he is speaking the truth. There is an enormous amount of research on the relationship between certainty, certainty of the witness, and how often the witness is correct -- and I'm not talking about two or three studies, but at least about a hundred or so. The bottom line of all those studies is that the relationship between certainty and correctness is very, very weak. There are many witnesses who are perfectly certain, and they are wrong. And there are many witnesses who are totally uncertain, but they are right. The bottom line is that the amount of certainty expressed is much more an aspect of the personality of that witness. Some are very certain witnesses -- that's the way they are -- and some other people are always uncertain, even when they know the answer perfectly well. It's more an aspect of personality than an aspect of the quality of what they saw or what they remember. So it's quite likely that an eyewitness is totally sincere, totally honest, very convinced, does not assume that he or she can make a mistake and still is very wrong about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, I think that we have mostly covered all the areas that you touched upon in your expert report, and so finally I should like to ask you to tell us your final conclusion, that is to say, to tell us what your opinion is as to the truthfulness and correctness of the identification of Vlatko Kupreskic done by Witness Q, on the basis of the facts that you had at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My conclusion is that the most important factor is the viewing distance, and the viewing distance is prohibitive for making a good, reliable recognition. My data show that some subjects in experiments that have been done are still able to do that, but more than 50 per cent are wrong. As I said, the question whether that sort of a risk in identification is acceptable is totally up to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Deviation from that, you said whether it was reliable, unreliable, the degrees of reliability?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. It's always difficult to express things in words that, to my mind, are perfectly well expressed in numbers. Whether, say, a probability of higher than 50 per cent that you are wrong, whether you would call that unreliable or slightly reliable or reliable, I think it's matter of words. What I have found is that to all probability, you must assume here that the likelihood of making a mistake at 60 metres, in the given conditions, is higher than 50 per cent. I don't call that reliable, but it's a matter of words. I would rather testify to the data that I have reported than to how you express that in words.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I think we have understood each other. Thank you very much, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions. I should just like to propose that these two documents be tendered into evidence as Defence Exhibits D58/3 and D59/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. And I see no objection from the Prosecution. They are admitted into evidence. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I think you were asking whether any other of the Defence counsel have any questions; I have one question for the Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor. I am counsellor Petar Pavkovic. Perhaps -- that is to say, I feel that this question should perhaps be given a broader, more complex answer, but I would be satisfied for the moment, and for these purposes, to remain at the level of a stand of principle. I should like to ask you briefly, and in principle, to tell us what the effect of time is, and the passage of time, on memory and the ability to reproduce what was once remembered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're perfectly right that you're asking a rather complicated question, because obviously the answer depends very much upon what it is you want to remember. Like, a telephone number can be forgotten within a few seconds, but the fact that you won a case, which can be announced to you in the same amount of time, you will probably remember your whole life. So it is not easy to say what time is doing to memory. Some things will simply be never forgotten; time is irrelevant. Some things are very quickly forgotten, and everything in between is also possible. Now, we know that remembering a face that you have never seen before is, indeed, influenced by time. Studies that we have done related to bank robberies show that, say, after six weeks, for instance, remembering the face of the bank robber becomes problematic. I'm talking about six weeks. But remembering that you have seen someone whom you have known all your life, so that you don't have to remember the face of a bank robber, but only the name of a person, for instance, if you were in a bank and suddenly one of your colleagues comes in and appears to be a bank robber, well, that's rather surprising to you, and you won't forget that; not within six weeks, not within six months, and not even within six years. Now, there is a second problem, which is what we call the problem of rehearsal. To some things in our life, we are reminded all the time, and that means that in our memories, these things are refreshed all the time. Now, if we refresh some memories every day, we are simply not forgetting those things. Other things, to which we are never reminded, may gradually disappear. Now, the problem with a face is that it's very difficult to refresh the picture of a face in your memory if you are not shown the picture. So if you have to remember the face of a bank robber, but they have not caught the culprit yet, so you are not confronted with that face, in the meantime, the witnesses may forget the faces because they are not refreshed. But if you have to remember a name, you can refresh that yourself. Every time you tell the story: "This is what happened to me, this person did that to me," the name is refreshed. It can happen several times a day. And then there's no reason why memory would fade at all. So there are two factors, I think, which makes it rather urgent that if you have a question, you should be rather specific, because in general, the question cannot be answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I'm satisfied with your answer. Everything else would require far more time and far more facts. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That is all I wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to ask a question now as to the inquisitiveness of the expert witness. My name is Luka Susak. I am the Defence counsel of Drago Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You mentioned the distance of recognition and the distance in viewing. I'm interested in knowing what is the greatest distance at which a person can be recognised? I have, of course, in mind that you said that sometimes there is absolute certainty, other times not, but I'm interested in hearing an answer. At what distance can an individual be recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's good that you ask this question, because it gives me an opportunity to point again to the table, which is just the result of one study but it explains the principle. If you look at recognition rate at a distance of three metres, which is as far apart as we are now, probably, what you see is that even with perfect illumination, recognition is not perfect. There's always a likelihood that someone makes a mistake. The more one person resembles another, the more likely that is. There is simply no situation in which, as a psychologist, I could say, "There, no mistakes are made." Only, in such conditions, that the likelihood of a mistake becomes very, very small, so that for daily use we can say it's perfect. On the lower side, at the very long distance it's not going to zero. It's very difficult to say there it's impossible to make a correct identification, because even by guessing, you might be right. So the question is not at what distance is it impossible to recognise a person. The question really is, I think, at what distance are recognitions not reliable enough to be used as evidence. I phrase it that way because part of the problem is with me, I can say something about the rate, rate of mistakes, and part of the problem is with you, as lawyers, because you determine what reliable evidence is. But it's not a question of perfect recognition or no recognition at all. We're always dealing with something in between, and always the question of what is reliable enough to a court must be addressed. But for all practical purposes, that's what I have published on this business. I would say that recognitions at distances below 15 metres are about the best that a Court can get. There's little hope that you can improve upon recognitions at distances below 15 metres. Above 15 metres is not perfect anymore, and if you want the best evidence, I would say then use recognitions at distances shorter than 15 metres. But I would never say all recognitions at distances above 15 metres are wrong, because they aren't. Above 15 metres, the question becomes how reliable do we want it to be. But that's your problem, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Another short question, and it will be more concrete. Can an individual be identified at 200 metres if they are sitting down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you explain to me what you mean by "if they are sitting down"? Do you mean the face of that person is visible, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, the face is visible but not the movements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In general, movement and posture are minor factors with respect to recognising a person. Unless a person has a very specific way of moving, for instance, because he's crippled or so, it is very difficult to recognise and very tricky to recognise a person from posture or movement. Really, the most important factor is the face, and if you look at studies that compare recognising living and moving persons with recognising the same person but only from a picture of their face, there's hardly any difference because the face is really decisive. With respect to posture and movement, there are so many people who have the same posture or move in the same manner that it's really rather tricky to accept identifications on the basis of those. So the question really is can you see the face, and as I have argued already for 60 metres, the likelihood that you would make mistakes at a distance of 60 metres is so high that I would never call that reliable, and at 200 metres it's obviously even worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Professor, I just asked for an answer to whether an individual can be recognised at 200 metres or not, an individual sitting down with their face visible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're bringing me in a somewhat difficult position by asking me "Yes" or "No," because what I have explained is, unfortunately, not a "Yes" or "No" thing. I would never say that if you see a person at 200 metres and you think, "This is so and so," that you would always be wrong. I'm only saying the likelihood of making a mistake at a distance of 200 metres is very, very high.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So as far as I was able to understand, an average person could recognise somebody sitting at a distance of 200 metres. I'm saying this out of my own curiosity, and I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. I'm Franck Terrier, one of the counsel for the Prosecution. As you have experience with trials, you are fully aware that I will now proceed with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: First of all, Professor, could you tell us whether you familiarised yourself with the transcripts that were communicated to you by Mr. Krajina, I believe; the trial records, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the letter I sent to Mr. Krajina, I identified the pages of the trial records that I have used for familiarising myself with the situation that I was to study.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Professor, in that case, you were able to correct two involuntary errors in the introductory letter of Mr. Krajina. The first is that he said that a group turned around when they were shot at and looked at the soldiers for a moment, and the second error being that those soldiers were 60 metres away. I should like to underline that it follows from the record that the group didn't turn around but some members of that group, and this could affect your answer to question number 6 or, rather, 8, I think. The second remark I should like to make, Professor, at the beginning of this cross-examination, is that the witness spoke of a distance of 50 to 60 metres, not a distance of 60 metres. I should also like to ask you to take into account the hypothesis that the distance might have been smaller than 50 or 60 metres, that it could have been 40 metres, because I should like to convey to the trial that we have new elements. That evidence is not presented in court now. I'm just presenting it in a hypothetical form to gain benefit from your experience and knowledge in these matters. So I am asking you to take into account this hypothesis of a distance of some 40 metres. I should like to check that I fully understood your conclusions. You say that regarding recognition of a person known from before, a familiar person, the risk of error in identification increases with the distance, and particularly when the distance increases to above 12 metres. And you say that at a distance of 40 metres, the ratio between hit and false identification is 1 to 1, that is, that the risk of error is 50 per cent. Did I understand you well, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If I take your last two points, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You also say, at the end of your letter to Mr. Krajina, I think, that 60 metres is four times the required distance for recognition to be considered acceptable, so that the required distance would be 15 metres. You also say that at 60 metres, identification remains possible, is still possible. To take up a question that has just been made by Attorney Susak in a slightly different manner, I should like to ask whether you can tell us, bearing in mind the physiological performance of the human eye, what is the maximum distance at which one can recognise a face without taking into account other factors, the memory suggestions and so on, simply the physiological performance of the human eye. What is the maximum distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I address all the points you have made in order, so that we start with the fact that they all turned around, or do you want an answer first to the last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: First the last question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I would say that the legal sciences are entirely different from my science. It would be highly interesting to study the physiological performance of the eye without memory and anything else. Unfortunately, in humans, the eye is connected to memory. We cannot disconnect it. It's not possible to answer the question of what the eye can do if not connected to the brain. It is connected to the brain, and it must be connected to the brain because recognition occurs in the brain, not in the eye. But at the same time, all other contributions that the brain can make are made during recognition. It cannot be helped. So as an example, your problem of at what distance can you recognise a person, take the following example: We know that through a door at 200 metres, say, two persons can enter. It's either you or the President of the Court and there are no other possibilities. I know that. Then at 200 metres, I will be quite safe in recognising whether it is the President of the Court or you, because I don't need to identify small details in the faces. I only need to identify very rough details and that's enough, and you are sufficiently different to do that at 200 metres. On the other hand, when two people who are more or less alike must be distinguished, I need to see details in their faces, and then it very soon becomes necessary to be at a distance of 15 metres. So the question is not what can the eye do but what information needs the eye, on top of other information that the brain already has, to make a correct identification. But it can't be helped that the problem is always that complicated, because we are not talking about the eye. The eye is only, say, the beginning of the process, it's the camera part, but the recognition is taking part in the brain on the basis of what information the eye is sending, and there's so much more information in the brain that the question cannot be answered in general. But if we are specific about the situation you are dealing with, which is people are fleeing, they are looking back, Witness Q is looking back, he sees four people, now the question is who are these people, and one he seems to recognise. Now, in principle, it could be a large number of people who are standing there. It's quite possible that they are people he's never seen before. But he seems to recognise one person he knows very well, and he is so certain about that that he testifies here in this Court it could not have been someone else. Well, in order to be reliable, you must make sure that it was not a person who looked rather like the person he knew before, and in order to do that, to make that distinction at a reliable-enough manner, he needs to resolve small details in the face, because there can easily be two people who look rather alike, but the details in the face differ when you look at small things like half a centimetre. So in my opinion, in order to give reliable evidence that it's this person he saw and not possibly any other person, he needed to resolve small details, and he could do that only at a distance of 15 metres or below. That's why I would say if you limit it to the question that you have here and not broaden it to very general questions about what people can do in all sorts of circumstances, you're talking about this condition, then I would say in this condition you need a distance of 15 metres or below. I'm sorry to give such long answers, but you're asking very complicated questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Professor, I listened to you with a great deal of attention and interest, but I'm still going to ask you another question which may be even more complicated. I see that there is a clear distinction, at least at this stage of our discussion, between the variables allowing one to say that recognition was precise or that there was a risk of error, and then on the other hand the question of reliability, that the reliability of recognition is something quite different. In my understanding, that is not up to the expert. It is not the responsibility of the expert but the responsibility of the Judges, who have to take into account other elements of assessment, among others, the fact that the presence of that recognised person in that spot was corroborated by other testimony, for instance. So the question of reliability is up to the Judges, whose sovereign right that is. At least that is my opinion. What I would like to look into are the variables which lead us to think that a recognition was precise or that there may be a certain percentage of error. So I come back to the question which I consider important, because in your reply, you mentioned considerations related to eye physiology. I think that an analysis is possible, because when we go to see an optician, we are asked to recognise A, B, C, and D, and we know that beyond a certain distance, we cannot recognise those letters. So my question is: Is there a distance beyond which recognition of a face is physiologically impossible because it is beyond the capacity of the eye, similarly to what we do when we visit an eye doctor and are asked to recognise letters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the example of the letters is a very good one to illustrate the problem that I have. At a very large distance, you may be presented with a letter, and if you just guess, you have a probability of 1 in 26 that you give the correct response. I, as a psychologist, cannot know what you did, whether you guessed or whether you saw it. I can only say if the distance increases, the performance levels go down to 1 in 26 correct, and probably they won't go down to zero. The same is with face recognitions. The performance goes down with distance, but they usually do not go down to zero because there is always other information in the head of witnesses that helps them to guess. Obviously, you don't want guessing witnesses. You want to get witnesses who testify to what they saw in a reliable manner, and therefore when you approach levels of performance that may be interpreted as just guessing performance, you should become very careful. You should become very careful even when the performance level is not zero, because the guessing level is above zero. Now, in the situation we are talking about, the question of guessing is not irrelevant, because if in that group of persons standing there and shooting there was someone he knew, how many could that have been, how many people were in the area? So if he felt, "I know some of them," then guessing might have led him to this observation, so the guessing level is a reality. The performance is not going down to zero. But quite rightly, you say that the only contribution that I can have is I can present you with some results of studies that we did. I hate to repeat myself, but the bottom line is, of course, I will never say that at distances, and we're not talking about miles and miles because obviously there is no recognition possible anymore, but at a distance we're talking about here, 60 metres, or 50, or 70, it doesn't matter so much, performance is still not at zero. It isn't. I can't help it. It's not at zero. But in the neighbourhood of 40 metres, already there are as many wrong identifications as correct identifications, and at longer distances, it's getting worse. Unfortunately, you're just, in your problem, hitting the area where it's not ideal, it's not even reliable, I would call, and it's not zero. I can't help it. That's the distance under discussion. That's how the situation grew. Obviously, it's the responsibility of the Court to say, "What criteria, with respect to eyewitness reliability, do we pose?" That's your problem. I can only sketch for you different likelihoods of making mistakes, and whether you think that's good enough, in the light of all the information that you have received in the meantime and I don't have, I will not and I cannot, of course, make that judgment for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand very well, Professor. I am going to put that question in a slightly different way. I am trying now to examine, and I'm asking you to say whether at a distance of some 60 metres, there is any obstacle linked to the physiology of the eye which makes recognition either impossible or extremely dangerous, and I'm referring to eye physiology again without referring to the brain or any interpretations. Going back again to the doctor's office, if the doctor asks me to recognise A, B, and Z, and if I'm trying to guess the letter, to guess the letter, that is only normal. Because this is an experimental situation, emotions, memory, feelings do not intervene or they do so to a minor extent, can we say that there is a physiological difficulty for the eye to recognise an object or the size of an object at a distance of 60 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If you refer to the letters in the office of the ophthalmologist, the technician, the answer is quite simple. The letters are constructed in such a way that you need to resolve, as we say, one minute of arc, and that's the density of cones in the retina. That means for observation at 60 metres, that the thickness of the lines, of the letters, needs to be two centimetres. At 50 metres, the letters of the doctor are half a centimetre. Now, the doctor does it in a different way. He keeps the distance constant, because you are staying where you are, and he changes the size of the letters, because that's more convenience than increasing the distance of the observer. But the rule is the same. You can't see the letters in the office of the optician if you cannot resolve one minute of arc, which coincides with the sizes that I gave you. These letters are, of course, specially constructed to make it very clear whether you can see them or not see them. Unfortunately, faces are not entirely like letters; they are not constructed for optimal distinction between seeing or not seeing. So the question is much easier for letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could we, for a moment, examine the table attached to the letter that you sent to Mr. Krajina. The two variables that were introduced are a distance of 3 to 40 metres, and illumination, 0,3 to 3.000 lux. Could you tell us what level of illumination corresponds to the daylight at 8.00 in the morning, to normal daylight, in the morning, in Europe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends on the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right, Professor. I'm talking of the month of April, in the northern hemisphere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then probably -- you're probably very close to 3.000, so it's -- the right-hand column represents normal daylight. 300, which is the step below, then you are already in the dusk, so normal daylight would be represented by 3.000, and it can be a lot brighter if you have bright sun. The problem is that what you can do in laboratory, where you try to control the conditions, the best you can achieve is something like 3.000, so that's why we didn't go any higher; but 3.000 is a fair representation of a normal day, if you're not on, say, a beach, in the burning sun.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And 2 lux corresponds to what illumination, now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't present a description of what it means. 0,3, the darkest, is in an area where there is no artificial illumination, in the night, with no moon. And then 2, you might say, is in the same area, with a very bad illumination, and then you slightly go on, gradually, to improving the situation. 2, 3, and 5 are especially included because many questions that arise in court is recognising people in city conditions, and at night, and 2, 3, and 5 are situations that you can encounter in city conditions at night, in various roadways, with a lot or not a lot of illumination. And that's why I chose 2, 3, and 5, closer to one another, because that's a relevant area, and then I go, with somewhat larger steps, to the lighter part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So to read correctly this table, we should say that at the level of 2 lux and a distance of 12 metres, we come across a figure of 2,6, which means two correct recognitions against six incorrect recognitions. Is that the way we should read these results in the table?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the numbers in the table are odds. They are always so much to 1. So the number that you mentioned is 2,6 to 1; 2,6 correct to 1 incorrect. It's always so much to 1. And if we go to the right, then at 10 lux, it's 28 to 1, and 67 to 1. Always so many correct to 1 incorrect. And what you see in the bottom line, where it goes below 1, so there, it can be like 0,2 to 1, which means 0,2 correct to 1 incorrect; that means far more incorrect to correct. So if the number is 1, the number of correct and incorrect identifications is the same, is equal. If you go below 1, there are more incorrect identifications than correct. And what you see at 3.000 lux, at a distance of 40, it's 0,8 to 1, which means it's almost 50-50. Almost 50-50. Slightly below, but that's not so important. These are, of course, experimental data.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Precisely, could you tell us what was the protocol of the trial that was applied in this test?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The protocol is that people see a face under these conditions, and then immediately, without any delay -- so it's a retention time of zero seconds, you may say -- they have to point out on the display whom they saw. The display may have the face that they saw. That's the situation of a line-up where the suspect is indeed guilty, and then you can make a hit, because if you point out the correct person, that's what's called a "hit." The other half of the subjects see a display of persons, and the one face they saw is not present. That's the situation of a line-up in which the suspect happens to be not guilty; that's not the person they saw before. In that case, they can make a false alarm; if they still point out someone, that's called a false alarm. The numbers represented in this table are the ratio of hits and false alarms. That's the ratio of correct identifications and mistaken identifications. In order to do that, you need the two conditions of what we call "target-present line-ups" and "target-absent line-ups."

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Who were the subjects who were looking, who were asked to identify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The subjects were students, so young people at our university, with perfect eyesight. So this is about the best subjects can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And the face that they were asked to recognise, was it a real face, or was it a photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As for the persons they knew from before and they were asked to recognise or not recognise, were they photographs of members of their family, or just people they knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, as I explained in my letter, they were photographs of people they did not know. I have explained that in my letter, in the point -- on page 2, at the bottom paragraph. "The results in the appendix represent ..." -- and so on. And what I have pointed out in that letter is that what I want to illustrate with these data is the sudden drop that occurs between 12 and 20 metres, because that drop is not related to anything in the brain, where the effect of persons known or not known to you is located, but to something in the eye. The eye cannot resolve the face any more, and that's why you get this sudden drop. If you're interested, you may compare the effect of what happens if you go from the right in the table to the left, where you go from much light to less light. There you see a gradual decrease of the numbers. There's not a sudden drop, because the eye does not react to lower light levels, a sudden drop, it's not a system of "go" and "no go." But if you go from the top to the bottom, there you see the sudden drop. You see it in all columns. It is there for 10 lux as well as for 3.000 lux, and that is because you cross a certain -- say, "go/no go" system in the eye. That's the point I wanted to illustrate, and that simple biological piece of information is true for faces that you know and you don't know. It's simply not resolved any more. The eye stops. That's the point illustrated in this table.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I go back to the protocol of the trial to ask you for two or three points of clarification. The photographs that these students were asked to recognise, were there several, or was it one photograph? Were there several photographs shown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a large number of photographs was used, of course, for several reasons. One is, if you ask a student to recognise a number of people and they're always the same, it becomes very easy, so you can't do that. The other is that the way you test their memory is you present them with a photographic line-up of faces, and you ask them to point out, "Which is the one you saw?" For that, obviously, you also need a large number of photographs to pick from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But my question was more specific. When this subject was shown a photograph, did he see only one photograph, or several in a line-up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The experiment, of course, consists of two stages. First you are confronted with one face, and then immediately thereafter, you are confronted with a photographic line-up in which you have to point out which of these people is the one you saw. So in step 1 you see one face, and in the next step you see a line-up of several faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As we are interested in the recognition of a person known from before, could you tell us, what was the type of link that existed among those people on the photographs and your subjects, your students?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I explained on page 2 of my letter, there's no link. That's not the purpose of this experiment, and it's not the reason why I refer to it. The reason is only that -- the sudden drop between 12 and 20 metres, where the eye cannot resolve faces any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand. You explained that in your letter. But we are interested in this very specific question, which is rather different from the one you dealt with in your trial, that is, recognition of a person known from before. Because now we, or rather I, have to try and check and verify whether this situation in the trial can be transposed to reality. I'm asking you, what were the faces which these students were asked to recognise? Whose faces were they? Were they film stars, people known? Was there an emotional link between those subjects and the photographs -- their mothers or fathers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No link, as I explained in my letter. There is no link. They are faces of people taken in a different city, so it's highly unlikely that they would ever have met these people before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you have a lot more questions, Mr. Terrier? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm afraid I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Because we have this problem with Judge May, who needs to preside over a hearing in another chamber. I understand, however -- yes? And then Mr. Par will probably have more questions, and I, too, have some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, take your time, because we have just decided to continue until 11.30, and I hope three-quarters of an hour will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I shall do my best, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Professor, I understood that the students were asked to identify photographs of people they knew. Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I explained -- I think I was rather careful to explain that -- in the bottom paragraph of page 2 of my letter: "The results in the appendix represent the identification of people not known before." Not known before. "There is a retention period of zero seconds, and it is therefore not wholly representative for the recognition of familiar people, but the sudden drop beyond a distance of 12 metres is highly relevant for the recognition of familiar people, because it represents a physiological limit of the human eye." That's the reason. So I don't think I left any uncertainty about that aspect. It is only the sudden drop that represents a mechanism in the eye that simply applies to all faces that you see, known or not known. If the eye cannot resolve them any more, then it stops, you see. Therefore, below -- the bottom part of the table is simply representing situations of faces that could not be resolved by the eye any more. Therefore, I think it's relevant to your question. It is within the limitation that I have expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But, Professor, when you speak of identification of a face, it is identification in relation to what reference system? What does that student have to recognise? It is obviously my fault that I have misunderstood you; you have probably expressed yourself very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this experiment, the subject sees a face for about half a minute. Immediately thereafter, so with zero seconds interval, he sees a line-up and has to indicate which person in the line-up is the same as the face he has observed for about half a minute. And what you see is that. If you see a face -- at 20 metres, for instance -- for half a minute, you have observed it as well as you could for half a minute. Immediately thereafter, you see that face again, but surrounded by some other faces, and you have to indicate who was it that I saw, that for instance, at an illumination level of 3.000, they are doing it about five times correct against one time wrong, whereas if it's 12 metres, they do it 90 times correct versus one wrong. That's a huge difference. It's an enormous step, an enormous loss of performance, and that loss of performance is related to the fact that the eye, during the first observation of half a minute, simply could not see the details in that face.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. However, I have a further question. In this experiment, the subject, the student, did he necessarily have to give an answer, or could he have doubts or incertitude? Could the student say, "I don't know"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, definitely. The experience is that very rarely subjects do that, I must say. If I may add something, it's always clear that an experiment is not exactly the same as being in a war. If you are asked about details of the experiment, we will always hit, of course, the fact that an experiment is somewhat artificial and that you cannot create conditions of war in an experiment. For some topics, like studying emotions, that is, of course, highly relevant because if you cannot recreate the correct emotions, then the experiment is worthless. But here we are dealing with, say, a biological property of the eye, in which I feel that exactly creating all sorts of conditions that are present in war is not necessary. What is necessary is recreating the biological conditions. Exactly like when you go to an optician, he presents you some letters to see whether you can see at a long distance. And then, if you take the glasses that he prescribed, you go to drive your car, you will not meet any letters any more, and still the glasses will work, because we're dealing with a biological mechanism that can be tested by letters, although you want to apply it on the highway. In the same manner, the reasoning applies -- at least to my mind -- that we present people with faces in a somewhat experimental condition, to test where the limit is that the eye can resolve. That limit will exist in wartime conditions equally well, because it's a biological piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And a last question regarding this table that you have submitted to us. Do I read it well by saying that at 3.000 lux, the ratio is below 1; when talking of a distance of 40 metres, it is 0,8; and at 2 luxes, which means very bad lighting, and still at a distance of 40 metres, the ratio is 4 to 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, you're right. And that illustrates, in a nice way, that the eye is connected to the brain. Since these numbers are ratios, there are two ways in which they can go down. One is that the upper part is going down or the lower part is going up. The lower part going up means false-alarm rates go up. Now, what happens in the 3.000 column is not only that the correct identifications go down, but also that the false alarms are going up, because people tend not to be so cautious when there is a lot of light, because they sort of have the feeling -- "There was lots of light. I had half a minute to look at this. It is rather silly for me not to recognise this face." So they have an inclination to give a response, instead of restraining themselves, as you have suggested is also an option. With 2 lux, they realise, "It's not so strange if I don't know the answer. The experimenter will not think I'm stupid if I say I don't know, because it's rather logical that I don't know." So at 2 lux, they don't make as many false alarms. And that piece of information is, of course, highly relevant for you, because what the Court has to decide is: This recognition that is presented in evidence, is that a hit, is that a correct identification, or may it be a false alarm? And what you should realise, that under daylight conditions, people tend to make false alarms. That's what I'm -- because these are conditions that, to themselves, present good viewing conditions, so they are prepared to make a response. That's the danger of daylight conditions, and that's why you have this difference. I'm sorry it is so complicated, but in fact, if you look at a simple thing like a recognition, rather soon you realise it's a complicated process. It has to do with the tendency to believe that you are in good viewing conditions and therefore it's not illogical for you to state firmly that you have recognised someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What I'm having difficulty with, Professor, is that, for reasons that are certainly justified, you have two series of considerations. First, the physiological performance of the human eye, and, secondly, the interference of the brain, memory, feelings, the psychological interference. I must admit that that is probably my own problem, that I'm sometimes having difficulty making a distinction between the two. I'm still surprised to see that there are far more errors, or false alarms, as you say, under conditions of perfect illumination of 3.000 lux, than with a very poor lighting of 2 luxes and at the same distance. I find this paradoxical, and I'm wondering whether psychological interferences are a sufficient explanation, because these two different illuminations, the eye physiology being affected by bad visibility, as everyone knows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I must excuse myself, because I did not anticipate that you would be interested in such a thorough discussion of these data, because then, of course, I would have supplied the complete publication. As you see, this is Table 7. There are tables which have separate representations of the hits and of the false alarms, so that you can exactly follow why these ratios change, and then you can see that the effect that you call paradoxical, indeed, is caused by the fact that people make false alarms under good viewing conditions and far less false alarms under difficult viewing conditions. You can see the same effect if you look at the difference between 3 metres and 5 metres. What you see at 3 metres, for 3.000 lux, you see that's not the best performance. It becomes slightly better at 5 metres, which is paradoxical. But that's not related to the hits; it's again related to the false alarm. Because if you saw a person at 3 metres, and then you say afterwards, "I don't recognise this person," then you look rather silly. So subjects have a tendency to at least point at someone, because they realise that the viewing conditions were perfect. And again, since the eye cannot be separated from the brain, we will always have such effects, but the sudden drop between 12 and 20 metres is really caused by a sudden decrease of the hits. So if you're interested, and if it's relevant for the proceedings of your Court, of course I would supply the complete publication so that you possess all the information that there is in it, although, in a sense, I would also like to warn you a little bit that what I'm saying about the eye is of course not only based upon this one publication. We know the density of cones in the retina perfectly well; there is simply no discussion. Any basic textbook will give you that sort of information. But if it's relevant to you, I would of course be glad to supply the whole publication, and you can split all those effects out. If you need more explanation, then later on, I would be happy to return and do that for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Forgive me for asking this question, but since you relied quite extensively, it seems to me, on your experimental findings to say that facts that have to be tried by this Chamber, recognition carries a serious risk of error. My role as Prosecutor finds this to be a very important point in the trial; not the only one, but very important, still. As a member of the Prosecution, it is up to me to see whether this experiment, and this experimental knowledge that you are conveying to us, allow us to read and understand the reality facing this Trial Chamber. In view of that, I am asking you whether -- don't you think that the relief of the face which is known, or which is to be recognised, the face in reality, such as it is, is it not an important element to be taken into consideration, and that this experiment, which you have conveyed to us, did not take that into account at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, sure, there's a number of things to be said about that issue. The experiment is based upon, say, a whole variety of faces, not on one face, so the data are telling you something about recognising human faces in general. If there's one particular face with very outstanding features, then of course -- and you have a reason to believe that everything would be different for that particular face -- then you should do experiments with subjects and that particular face specifically, which can be done, of course. What I have done, however, is describe what would happen, and what the risks are, if we are talking about a face that is just a normal human face, with not such distinctive features that you would say for this particular face, everything would be different. And I have found no information, in the documentation that I have received, that we're dealing with a very specific, remarkable face with outstanding features, and I have no way to make a judgment about that. I have not even seen a picture of the person that was seen, so I have no judgment about it. But if you have reason to believe that everything would be different for this particular face, I think then you should request a specific study for that face. However, I still would like to warn you that at 60 metres, if you think that a specific face would be highly and reliably recognisable at 60 metres, it should be really a remarkably different face, with large details that are different from normal. To give you an example, if a person is a cyclop, has one eye in the middle of the front, that can be seen at 60 metres, rather obviously. But a rather big nose would already be difficult, because even big noses are not so big, so it should be a remarkably big nose. But I have simply no information about the specific face that we are discussing here. To make any judgment about that, I think it's your judgment to see whether there is reason to request a specific study, or at least reject this study. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Professor, I wasn't really speaking about a face with recognisable features, and still less a monster. My question is: Is it really the same thing to look at a photograph and to look at a real person at the same distance? Is it quite the same thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, of course, we have studied that before running such an experiment, so one part -- also reported in this publication, I think, if you would have a complete copy -- is that first, of course, we made a comparison of seeing the real person and seeing a photograph of that person, under these conditions, to see whether that would not make a difference. Of course, the advantage of using photographs instead of real persons and presenting real line-ups all the time, instead of photograph line-ups, the advantage is so big that if you can do that, and you understand that this is a table that represents six, seven times nine experiments, in each cell is one experiment, so it's a huge study. So if you can do that with photographs, it's such an advantage that you would always do it, if its possible. Therefore we ran a pilot study to see whether the results would be any different if you used real faces, real persons, instead of photographs. The results were equal, so I don't think that is a particular problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: For example, the context in which a face is to be recognised, can the background have any effect? Is it the same to recognise a face with a white background or with a forest in the background? Does the background play a role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, definitely, definitely. Here we have used backgrounds with optimal contrasts, so that's the best possibility of recognising the faces. It's very easy to make it more difficult. For instance, say one important feature of people is their hairstyle, and if you use a background of the same colour as the hair, it becomes very difficult to recognise the hairstyle, and then one important feature is lost. These data reflect optimal conditions in which things like the hairstyle, for instance, can be optimally seen, so you can easily make it much more difficult and the results get worse. Since I have simply no information about the background against which, say, in your case the face was seen, you really need a careful reconstruction, because if people are standing in front of a house, if they stand in front of the white wall of the house, it's totally different than if they stand in front of the black window of the house. Still, the distance would be 50 centimetres to the right or to the left. So I have not even tried to reconstruct for myself what the situation would be. I've only looked at let's assume that it's optimal. Then still we've got this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like to go back to the effect of fear and danger that you referred to. You said, if I understood you correctly, that a situation of fear and danger can limit the field of observation, while at the same time increasing the attention, the focusing of that subject on that field of vision. I wanted to ask you, and I think you already have answered up to a point --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, my client would like to be excused for a moment, if he may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you to tell us whether this effect which you have explained, that of fear and danger, is valid for all individuals, for all persons, or, on the other hand, are certain persons prone to lose all their capacity of observation in a situation of fear and danger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to begin with, I think I have clearly stated that on the matter of fear, I have no opinion on what effect it could have had in this particular case.
