It could have improved the observation, and it could have worsened the situation. I have simply no idea, because it's very difficult to predict where the witness would look. Now, individual differences are mostly influencing the question whether, in a particular situation, a person will have fear, because if you are used to a situation, you might have less fear than if that situation is completely new to you. So individual differences are related mostly to in which situations will the fear occur. But given the same amounts of fear in various people, the effects will be more or less the same. So the question in this case would be, "How much fear will there be in this particular witness," and I have no way of knowing that. I don't even know the witness. The question is not so much, "And if there was fear, would there be the same effect as in other people," because these effects of fear are rather universal. The biggest difference with respect to people is some have fear and some don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying, but I should like to respectfully note that they are not responsive to my question. To go back to the facts that we have to judge, this was indisputably a situation of danger, because the group of people who were being shot at were escaping, about to flee, and they were exposed to threat. None of them were armed. They were all civilians. Some were women, others were children. So without any doubt, we're facing a situation of danger. Let us not speak of fear. Let us just focus on the question whether this situation of danger, which is undisputed, what effect it could have had on the capacity of observation and attention of those people, and did it differ depending on the personality of each? Of course, I'm not asking you to analyse the individual effect, but could there have been a difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The difference, if you assume the same amount of danger and therefore -- which is not a necessity, but let's just, for the sake of argument, assume the same amount of fear in these people, then there is still the question, "What will they focus on?" One person may focus on the arms that are pointed at them, and other people may focus on the faces behind those arms, which is a different thing. Others may even focus on totally different areas where they expect that some other danger will come from. So the differences with respect to how people would react, given that they have the same amount of fear, in my opinion would in the first place be on what will they focus on. To give a very simple example, it has nothing to do with emotions and it happens to me all the time, if I'm visiting other people and I come back, my wife always knows what the other women were wearing and I don't. I've seen the same, but I've not focused on the same. There is some difference between men and women with respect to what they pay attention to. Now, obviously since we're here, we're talking about men, women and children. They may pay attention to different things, and then the fear, that will have a remarkable effect, because paying attention to the one thing rather soon means that you did not pay attention to the other things. So, indeed, you're quite right, there may be huge differences as to what they paid attention to. The only thing I want to stress is that for me, as an expert, it's not a subject I can really tell you much about because I have no basis for deciding whether the witness in this case paid a lot of attention to that face or not. It's quite possible that he paid a lot of attention to that face. It's also possible that he didn't. I have no way of knowing. That's not a question, I think, that you can pose to an expert who was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes. But, Professor, don't we have there the answer to the question number 6 posed to you by Mr. Krajina, why other people in the same group did not recognise the face in question? You said that it was due to the distance. Couldn't the answer simply be because other people may have been looking at something else, their attention may have been drawn to some other details?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're quite right. It's quite possible that these other people were not looking at this face. But what I wanted to say is that even if they had concentrated on this face, still the distance of 60 metres would have made it rather unlikely that they would have recognised anyone. Maybe it's a bad habit of scientists, but if there's a simple answer that makes it not necessary to go into the more difficult things, then we are always quite satisfied and say, "Well, we take the simplest argument, and that relieves us of going to a far more difficult thing about which I can tell you very little. So why would I speculate on the more difficult thing if I can tell you something that's rather reliable on the simple question of distance?" So you're quite right, and if you want to make that speculation, I'm the last person to stop you. I can only say I have no way of knowing where these people looked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I will not engage in any kind of speculation, Professor. I'm just trying to take advantage, from your experience and your knowledge, to be able to better interpret the extremely complicated real situation that this Trial Chamber has to judge. Now to go to another question, the question of the degree of familiarity between the person who is doing the observation and the person to be recognised. Wouldn't a high degree of familiarity facilitate, at a distance of 40 or 50 or 60 metres, the recognition of the face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would say beyond a certain level of familiarity, the differences are not so important anymore. There are large numbers of people whom we know and whom we will recognise in half a second, and they don't have to be more familiar to be recognised by us. So degrees of familiarity, at least they have not been studied, so on the basis of scientific research, there's very little to say about it. But I think I have to come back to the same statement again. Even if there is a high degree of familiarity, beyond a certain distance you're going to make mistakes. In the end, you may even think that at a certain distance that person is your wife, and she isn't. Some distances are simply too long for reliable identifications. Another problem is, of course, that -- but I don't want to complicate the matter, of course -- we're talking here about a familiar person in a rather unfamiliar situation, and I don't know much about, and I've also written that in my letter, about, for instance, any head gear the person was wearing or anything unusual about the person whom you knew under different conditions, so I find it very hard to address the issue of familiarity at all without much more information about that exact situation. Therefore, again I would come back to the essential statement that 60 metres is simply prohibitive for reliable identifications anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: My question was the following: You told us that at 60 metres, identification is not impossible but it carries a risk of error. My question was whether a considerable degree of familiarity that we are going to suppose between the subject and the witness does not reduce that risk of error.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not necessarily, and we have to go back to the problem of hits and false alarms. High familiarity, in the first place, means that it is a response that is rather on the front of your mind. It's one of the responses you would first make rather than another response, which means that familiarity may increase the number of hits, which means if it is really the person you think it is, you are more likely to identify him, but if it's not him, are you more likely to make a false alarm, and therefore not necessarily the ratio of the two will go up. But this is a theoretical answer, of course. I understand that. But there is simply no research in which, say, degrees of familiarity are used in an experiment to see what exactly hits and false alarms will do. I will only warn you not to assume that just for logical reasons, say, the numbers should go up. It could go down as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Professor, you told us and you have written in your report that the pertinent features that the eye has to resolve to be able to make recognition are typically 0,5 centimetres, and you added that the smallest details which can be resolved by the human eye at a distance of 60 metres are of the order of two centimetres, and therefore we are facing a physiological difficulty there. I would like to ask you, and I address you as a psychologist and your professional experience in the field, what are the features of a face which need to be seen and recognised to permit identification, and do all features in the face contribute equally to an identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I seem to remember we've been through this. We had discussions of the nose and that sort of thing. I'm just wondering how helpful this is to the Chamber, to go into all this detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: My question, Your Honour, was the following: The expert has told us that details of a certain size need to be identified. My question was, "Which are the features and characteristics of a face that need to be recognised, and what should their size be for that identification to be possible?" It seems to me, and maybe I'm wrong, maybe I'm going beyond my duties here, but it seems to me that I can contribute, to a certain degree, to a better understanding of this matter by Your Honours. I think that this is a question that can be usefully put to the witness, but of course if you consider it quite useless, I will withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a matter for you and I'm not going to stop you, but please allow some common sense in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Professor, as a psychologist, could you tell us which are the facial features that need to be identified for recognition to be possible and whether these features, in themselves, contribute to an identification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a lot of misunderstanding about what is important to recognise a face, because people tend to believe that it is the eye or the nose or the mouth or something, whereas in fact it's the relationships between those things, the distance between things, the distance between the eyes, the distance of the eyes related to the size of your head and so on, so it's a matter of perceiving the relationships and not perceiving, say, eyes or noses. A slight change in relationships, placement of things, makes things totally different. So it's very hard to say, "Well, I saw the eyes. That's enough," or, "I saw the nose. Isn't that enough?" It's the relationship between things that matters most, that makes it so intangible to describe. If you ask a witness, "Well, you recognised him. How did you recognise him, then," or, "What did you recognise then?" Sometimes witnesses answer those questions, "I recognised the eyes," or, "I recognised the nose," but, in fact, witnesses don't know what they need to recognise a face because it's relationships between things in the face, and that's rather abstract. That's where half centimetres matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let me put my last question to you, Professor, and that is related to suggestion. You said that the recognition of a person that one knows from before is an immediate phenomenon, and a question put to you by Mr. Krajina, you said that suggestion plays a role, relating this to the fact that the witness did not immediately give to his interlocutors the name of the person that he recognised. In the circumstances that you familiarised yourself with, the circumstances of the time and place, does it seem really unusual that the witness did not immediately inform the people around him of the name of the person that he had recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, you're quite right. It would have helped a lot if I would have known that immediately he said or cried, "It's so and so," because that would mean there's an immediate recognition, and after that, there is no inference of suggestion anymore because the recognition is made, period. Now, I am in a situation in which I was told that he reported it much later. On that basis, I cannot decide whether he recognised immediately or not. I only know he did not report it immediately. It's impossible for me to decide whether he recognised immediately but had good reasons not to give away his information or he recognised not immediately but gradually became aware of what he had seen. I cannot make that distinction on the basis of what is provided to me, and it's a highly-relevant question and I think you have to answer it. But on the basis of the information I was given, I can't answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, the silence of the witness for a certain period of time, in itself, doesn't necessarily mean that he was under any suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It opens the possibility. It has to be sorted out, what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor, for having answered my questions. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Terrier. Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: No more questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions? I'm afraid I have a short question. Professor Wagenaar, I have realised that you have focused on the face of the person to be recognised, and at one point, I took some notes, you played down movement and posture. I wonder whether this is because you were under the influence of your own study, which was about faces and faces on photographs, because speaking as a layman, as a man on the street and of my own experience as somebody who is used to walking not here but in another place very similar to the country we are talking about, where there are hills and woods and so on, I can say that very often you can see from a distance, say even 50, 60, 70 metres, people whose face is not very clear, but then one may pay attention to the fact whether the person is short, is tall, is bald or has a lot of hair, but even more important, were they slim or fat or burly, so it is this combination which may prompt me to say, "Aha, well the face is not so very clear, but his whole body does match this name," of course on the assumption that this person is familiar to me, a person whom I have seen for ten years, for instance, in that particular area. So this is what happens to me, for instance, when I walk in Tuscany sometimes and I see people, and as I say, because of this combination of various elements, I am in a position to recognise this person. So my question is: Is it proper and correct to also emphasise the role of the other elements which, together with the face, may allow you, enable you, to say, "Yes, this is the man whom I know and he is there up on the hill, and I can see him even if he's in a wood, in a clearing in a wood, but I can see him fairly well"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, you're quite right, Your Honour, that such facts exist. But I focused, I hope, not so much on the studies I did, but on the situation as it was presented to me, and the following features are important: There are a number of people standing there at a distance of 60 metres. Now, to decide what their size is, you need some sort of reference. It's not obvious to me that a good reference point was available so that you could see whether they were short or tall. The size of people is very hard to distinguish if you have no reference point. The following point is that I have no information that the size of the person who was observed is remarkable in any way, which means that even if you perceive the size correctly, that doesn't mean that it definitely must be that one person, because if many people have the same size, then still it doesn't help you so much to perceive size correctly with the aid of reference points. The same as for posture. You're quite right, some people are highly recognisable because of their posture, because they are fat or slim or crooked or whatever. The question is if someone is just normal, falls on the average, how could you recognise such a person on the basis of posture? And experimental data shows that that is very, very difficult. The experiments run, more or less, as follows: You make a comparison of recognition scores in a number of situations. One is life, moving. One is life, stationary, so movement is excluded. The next is on television, moving. Then on television, stationary. Then on a photograph, total body, and finally on the photograph, only face. What you see, if you compare those conditions, that the differences are very small. The contribution of movement, posture, size, are really very small compared to what you can tell from a face. Now, a further condition is here, that I was told he looked in a moment, and the question is how much movement of people can you see in a moment if you're talking about one fixation, and that's what I have reported in my letter. In one fixation, you can't see any movement, you just see a still picture, and then there is very little to tell about movement. So I have not concentrated about these elements of what I was to say, because the face is so much more important than the other things in this situation that I think perceiving the face would be decisive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much. I assume there is no objection to the witness being released. Professor Wagenaar, we are most grateful to you for testifying in court today, and you may now be released. Before we adjourn, let me simply remind the parties that we will reconvene on the 21st of June for one week. We will then skip the following week, and then we will resume our proceedings on the 5th of July until the 23rd of July, just as a reminder. So the hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 11.35 a.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of June, 1999, at 9.00 a.m. 25
